title: Time Zones
objective: After this level you can explain why the world has time zones and where the calendar date changes.
summary: Earth turns 15° an hour, so the world uses 24 time zones counted from Greenwich. The date changes at the International Date Line, near 180°.

cards.headline: Call a friend on the far side of the world and you might be calling tomorrow.
cards.body: It's Monday evening where you are, and your friend is eating breakfast on Tuesday. Nobody's clock is broken. The planet is round, and it spins.

cards.headline: Every town had its own noon
cards.body: Earth turns 360° in about 24 hours, which is 15° of longitude every hour. So the Sun reaches its highest point at a slightly different moment in every town. For centuries, communities set their clocks by their own Sun. That worked fine until railways spread, and a timetable had to juggle a different local time at every stop.

cards.headline: Twenty-four slices of time
cards.body: The fix was standard time. Cut the globe into 24 zones along meridians 15° apart, counted from Greenwich, and make each zone one hour apart. The system was adopted at the same 1884 conference that picked the prime meridian. On a real map, though, the borders zigzag, bending to follow countries' borders.

cards.headline: Where tomorrow begins
cards.body: Keep adding hours as you travel around the world and the days stop adding up. Something has to reset the calendar. That's the International Date Line, which roughly follows the 180° meridian, halfway around the world from the prime meridian. Cross it heading west and your calendar jumps a day ahead; head east and you get yesterday back. It even bends around the islands of Kiribati, so the whole country shares one date.

mascot.line: Head east over the line and you get yesterday back. I'd use mine to finish yesterday's crossword.

cards.headline: Time zones: sorted
learned: Earth turns 15° of longitude every hour
Zone borders bend to follow countries
The date line, near 180°, is where the date changes

questions.prompt: How many degrees of longitude does Earth turn every hour?

options.rationale: Much faster than that: 360° in about a day.
24 is the number of hours, not degrees per hour.
That would be a full turn in 4 hours.

questions.explanation: 360° in about 24 hours works out to 15° every hour, which is why time zones are 15° wide.

questions.prompt: You fly west across the International Date Line. What happens to your calendar?

options.label: It stays the same
options.rationale: Crossing the line always changes the date.

options.label: It moves one hour ahead
options.rationale: That's a time zone; the date line changes the day.

questions.explanation: West of the date line is one calendar day ahead, so heading west you skip forward a day.

questions.prompt: From Level 3: the date line sits halfway around the world from which line?

options.label: The Equator
options.rationale: The Equator runs east to west; the date line runs pole to pole.

options.label: The Arctic Circle
options.rationale: That's a line of latitude near the North Pole.

questions.explanation: The prime meridian through Greenwich is 0° longitude; the date line roughly follows 180°, the opposite side.
